items.title: Do Not Give Out When Experiencing Trials
items.answer:
Jeremiah had every reason to give out. He watched Jerusalem burn, he watched people starve, and he himself was beaten, put in stocks, and lowered into a muddy cistern — all for faithfully delivering Jehovah's messages. If anyone had a licence to quit, it was him. Yet right in the middle of his book of sorrows, he picks up his pen and writes some of the most hopeful words in the Bible. Why? Because even while he was still suffering, he focused on what Jehovah had already done for him and for his people. That is the secret of not giving out when we experience trials. The workbook has built this part around four lessons from Lamentations chapter 3 — appreciate, trust, wait, and keep praying in faith — so let's take them one at a time, because each one answers a different way that trials try to crush us.

FIRST: APPRECIATE WHAT JEHOVAH HAS DONE FOR YOU. Jeremiah writes: "It is because of Jehovah's loyal love that we have not come to our finish, For his mercies never end." (La 3:22) Think about what he is saying. His people were still hungry. Still displaced. Still mourning their dead. But they were not FINISHED. Why not? Because of Jehovah's loyal love. The same is true of us today. Whatever we have lost — health, a job, a loved one, financial security — there are things we still have that no trial can take: we are still in Jehovah's hand, we still have the congregation, we still have the hope of everlasting life, and we still have a relationship with the almighty Creator of the universe. Not one of those is something we earned. Every single one is mercy.

Try a simple exercise this week — and I say 'try' because it works. Instead of listing only what your trial has taken from you, write a short list of what Jehovah has already given you and already carried you through. A sister in one congregation once did exactly that after her husband left her and her health collapsed in the same year. She said that when she finished writing — the congregation that surrounded her, the hope she had not had when she was in the world, the prayers that were answered even that week — the trial had shrunk back to its real size. It had not disappeared. But it was no longer the biggest thing in her life. Jehovah was. That is appreciation doing its work.

SECOND: TRUST THAT JEHOVAH WILL CONTINUE TO BE WITH YOU. The very next verse says: "They are new each morning; your faithfulness is abundant." (La 3:23) Notice that Jeremiah is not just remembering yesterday's mercies — he EXPECTED fresh mercies the next morning, and the morning after that. Jesus built on exactly the same thought: "So never be anxious about the next day, for the next day will have its own anxieties. Each day has enough of its own troubles." (Mt 6:34) Notice that Jesus does not promise a trouble-free today. He promises that today's supply of strength will cover today's troubles. Jehovah's care is delivered in daily portions, like the manna in the wilderness — you could not store it up, but it always arrived.

When a trial drags on, we tend to pile tomorrow's worries on top of today's: 'How will I cope next month? What if next year is worse?' But that is borrowing trouble from a day that has not arrived. Imagine a brother whose company announces layoffs. If he spends the whole night rehearsing a future he cannot control, he gets no rest — yet his children are fed today, his meetings happened today, his prayers were heard today. Jehovah's mercies showed up on schedule this morning. Trust means believing they will show up tomorrow morning too — and leaving tomorrow with Jehovah until it comes.

THIRD: WAIT PATIENTLY FOR YOUR TRIALS TO END. Look at verse 24: "Jehovah is my share," I have said, "that is why I will show a waiting attitude for him." (La 3:24) Jeremiah could not fix Jerusalem's ruin, and he could not rush Jehovah's relief. So he chose to do the thing he COULD do: he made Jehovah his share and resolved to wait for him. He adds: "Good it is to wait in silence for the salvation of Jehovah." (La 3:26) And in the same chapter he tells us why the waiting is safe: "For Jehovah will not cast us off forever. Although he has caused grief, he will also show mercy according to his abundant loyal love. For it is not in his heart to afflict or grieve the sons of men." (La 3:31-33) Did you hear that? It is NOT in his heart to grieve you. Correction and discipline may last for a time — compassion is his default setting.

Imagine a brother who has prayed about an unbelieving relative for over twenty years. He has invited her, written to her, answered her objections gently, and nothing has changed. Waiting for him looks like this: he keeps the door open, he keeps the kindness going, he keeps mentioning Jehovah at the right moments, and he keeps asking Jehovah for her — while refusing to conclude that she is beyond hope. That is 'a waiting attitude.' And if relief has not come yet in one of your own battles, remember that Jeremiah spoke these words while the ruins were still smoking around him.

Some of our trials also have no quick fix — a long illness, a prodigal family member, a financial situation that simply will not improve no matter what we do. Waiting is not doing nothing. While we wait on Jehovah, we keep praying to him in faith, we keep doing what we can, and we keep coming to the meetings, where our hope gets refilled week by week. And there is a promise attached: "Good is Jehovah to the one hoping in him, to the person who keeps seeking him." (La 3:25) Good things come to the one who keeps seeking him WHILE he waits.

FINALLY, notice how the chapter ends the stretch we read today: "You drew near in the day that I called you. You said: 'Do not be afraid.'" (La 3:57) That is Jeremiah's testimony AFTER it all. Notice — he does not say 'you removed my trial.' He says 'you drew near.' For a servant of Jehovah, that is the victory: not the trial ending, but the friendship holding through it.

So, brothers and sisters: whatever trial is weighing on you right now, do not give out. Appreciate what Jehovah has already done for you — the mercies you did not earn. Trust that his mercies will be new tomorrow morning, exactly on time. Wait patiently for your relief, keeping on praying to him in faith the whole while, confident that it is not in his heart to grieve you forever. The same loyal love that did not let Jeremiah come to his finish will not let us come to ours either.

Before we conclude, one honest caution: these four lessons are not a formula that guarantees quick relief. Some trials will only end in the new world. Jeremiah himself did not see Jerusalem rebuilt. But the lessons still held: he was not cast off forever, his mercies kept arriving each morning, and his relationship with Jehovah survived everything Babylon could throw at it. In the end, that proved to be worth more than the things the trial had cost him — and it will prove the same for us.

So, brothers and sisters, let's take these words home with us this week. When discouragement whispers that we are finished — remember La 3:22: it is because of Jehovah's loyal love that we have NOT come to our finish. When tomorrow looks frightening — remember La 3:23 and Mt 6:34: today's mercies cover today's troubles, and tomorrow's mercies will be new. When relief is delayed — remember La 3:24-26: make Jehovah your share, and show a waiting attitude. And through it all, keep praying to him in faith, because 'Jehovah drew near in the day that I called' (La 3:57). The same loyal love that did not let Jeremiah come to his finish will not let us come to ours either.

They are new each morning; your faithfulness is abundant.
So never be anxious about the next day, for the next day will have its own anxieties. Each day has enough of its own troubles.
“Jehovah is my share,” I have said, “that is why I will show a waiting attitude for him.”
Good it is to wait in silence for the salvation of Jehovah.
Good is Jehovah to the one hoping in him, to the person who keeps seeking him.

For Jehovah will not cast us off forever. Although he has caused grief, he will also show mercy according to his abundant loyal love. For it is not in his heart to afflict or grieve the sons of men.

items.title: Spiritual Gems
items.answer:
What I learned from this week's Bible reading (Lamentations 3-5):

1. Jehovah can use hardship during youth as valuable training. The focused gem verse says: "Good it is for a man to carry the yoke during his youth." (La 3:27) A yoke is a training tool — a young ox wears it so it learns to work alongside its master. Hardships we experience while we are young can train us to be patient, compassionate and dependable long before we hold any privilege of service. What feels like a burden now may be building exactly the qualities Jehovah will use later.

2. Honest self-examination is the road back to Jehovah. "Let us examine and scrutinize our ways, and let us return to Jehovah." (La 3:40) And notice verse 41: "Let us lift up our hearts along with our hands to God in the heavens." Examining our ways is not meant to leave us crushed — it is meant to send us back up to God, heart and hands together.

3. When everything around us collapses, Jehovah's throne does not. "As for you, O Jehovah, you sit enthroned forever. Your throne is for generation after generation." (La 5:19) Jerusalem's temple, walls and monarchy were gone — yet Jeremiah anchors the book's closing prayers on the one thing that could never be destroyed: Jehovah's rule.

Practical examples from these scriptures — how they have helped, or can help:
• La 3:27 helps me as a parent or youth counsellor: instead of resenting the pressures young ones face — school, peer pressure, health struggles — I can help them see that Jehovah is preparing them through it, the way a yoke trains a young animal for years of useful service.
• La 3:40 helped me at work: after a conflict with a colleague I wanted to relive every wrong thing they said. Sitting down to 'scrutinize my own ways' first — what did I say, how did I say it — turned a grudge into an apology and the relationship recovered.
• La 5:19 helps when discouraging news piles up — wars, economic hardship, sickness among friends. Before checking the headlines again, I read that one verse and remember whose world this really is and who is sitting on the throne.
• La 3:40-41 together remind me that repentance involves both heart and action — feeling sorry 'in the heart' but also lifting up my hands, that is, acting on what I have examined.

scriptures.quote: Good it is for a man to carry the yoke during his youth.
Let us examine and scrutinize our ways, and let us return to Jehovah.
Let us lift up our hearts along with our hands to God in the heavens:
As for you, O Jehovah, you sit enthroned forever. Your throne is for generation after generation.

items.title: Bible Reading — La 3:19-42 (th study 12)
items.answer:
Context: Jeremiah recounts his own affliction — bitterness and homelessness — yet in the middle of his grief he recalls Jehovah's abundant loyal love and mercy, which are new every morning, and he resolves to wait on Jehovah. He then calls on the people to examine their ways and return to Jehovah.

Lesson 1: Even in deep suffering, we can choose to focus on Jehovah's loyal love (La 3:22, 23). Lesson 2: A waiting attitude is not a broken spirit — it is confident hope that Jehovah acts at the right time (La 3:24-26).

Possible comment: "Let us examine and scrutinize our ways, and let us return to Jehovah." (La 3:40) Jeremiah wrote this while his whole world was in ruins. Instead of sinking into bitterness, he turned the crisis into a mirror. When a trial exposes weaknesses in us, that same mirror is open to us too: examine, return, and Jehovah — who is good to the one hoping in him — is ready to receive us.

scriptures.quote: Let us examine and scrutinize our ways, and let us return to Jehovah.
Good is Jehovah to the one hoping in him, to the person who keeps seeking him.

items.title: Starting a Conversation — House to House (lmd lesson 5 point 4)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 5 point 4 — “Do not be quick to correct a person. Allow him to express himself freely. If he says something that conflicts with Bible teachings, resist any urge to argue. ( Jas. 1:19 ) By listening to him, you gain insight into his viewpoint.— Prov. 20:5 .”

HOUSE TO HOUSE — Daniel shares a Bible truth from appendix A of the Love People brochure. The demonstration is conducted around the point: Ruth expresses a belief that conflicts with the Bible, Daniel does not correct or argue, he listens first, gains insight into what is really on her heart, and then tactfully shares the truth she actually needs.

Daniel (Publisher): "Good afternoon! I'm Daniel, one of your neighbours from the next street. Do you have a minute?"
Ruth (Householder): "A minute, maybe. Come in out of the sun."
Daniel (Publisher): "Thank you. I won't take long. I like to visit with our neighbours now and then, because my wife and I have found real comfort from the Bible — especially about family."
Ruth (Householder): "That's nice, but honestly, after losing my mother last year, I've settled my mind. I believe she's still around us — watching over me and the children. That's how I stay comforted."
Daniel (Publisher): (listens attentively, nodding) "So your mother meant everything to you. You must miss her terribly."
Ruth (Householder): "Every day. She was my best friend."
Daniel (Publisher): "I can hear how much you loved her. You know, the Bible itself talks about a man who lost loved ones and felt just as you do — Job. What you've told me helps me understand what you need. May I show you one thought from the Bible?"
Ruth (Householder): "Go ahead."
Daniel (Publisher): "It's in John 5:28: 'Do not be amazed at this, for the hour is coming in which all those in the memorial tombs will hear his voice.' In other words, the dead are not around us somewhere — they are resting safely in God's memory, waiting. And he promises to bring them back. Your mother's comfort is not gone forever; it's waiting for her."
Ruth (Householder): "Hmm... so the Bible actually says she could come back?"
Daniel (Publisher): "It does — and this tract explains it from the Bible, with all the scriptures. Please read it when things are quiet. May I come back next week and hear what you think?"
Ruth (Householder): "Alright, that's fair. See you next week."

Keys: Daniel followed lmd lesson 5 point 4 exactly. When Ruth said her dead mother was watching over her — a teaching that conflicts with the Bible — he did not correct her and did not argue. He let her express herself freely, and by listening he gained insight into her viewpoint: her real need was comfort over losing her mother. Only then did he share a simple Bible truth from appendix A of the Love People brochure — truth 30, 'Dead loved ones will be resurrected' — the one truth that speaks directly to what she feels, delivered with tact, not with correction.

scriptures.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: Everyone must be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger,
Do not be amazed at this, for the hour is coming in which all those in the memorial tombs will hear his voice
The thoughts of a man's heart are like deep waters, But the discerning man draws them out.

items.title: Starting a Conversation — Informal Witnessing (lmd lesson 4 point 3)
items.answer:
lmd lesson 4 point 3 — “Do not be condescending. Avoid giving the impression that you know everything and that the other person knows nothing. Speak with him in a respectful way.”

INFORMAL WITNESSING — Daniel offers a tract without ever talking down to the person, conducting the demonstration around the point: he treats the householder as someone who already knows her Bible and speaks to her respectfully as an equal.

Daniel (Publisher): (in the market) "Good afternoon! You look like a woman who doesn't waste time — two heavy baskets already."
Ruth (Householder): (laughs) "Market day waits for nobody, my brother."
Daniel (Publisher): "True! Say, I couldn't help noticing you were reading something on your phone just now."
Ruth (Householder): "Ah, my Bible app. I read my Bible every day. I've been in church since I was a girl."
Daniel (Publisher): "That's a wonderful habit — and it shows. You know, most people don't read their Bible at all, and here you are reading it at the market."
Ruth (Householder): "Well, I try. Though sometimes the things I read confuse me. My pastor says one thing, another church says the opposite."
Daniel (Publisher): "I can imagine that's frustrating — you clearly take the Bible seriously, so those contradictions must really bother you. I've felt the same, which is why I was glad when I found a way to let the Bible explain itself."
Ruth (Householder): "Oh? How do you mean?"
Daniel (Publisher): "I have a small tract here — 'How Do I Choose My Friends?'... actually, the better one for you is this one about the Bible itself. It's short, and it doesn't tell you what to think — it shows you questions to ask the Bible directly. Someone with your reading habit could work through it in a sitting. I don't claim to have all the answers myself — far from it — but between your Bible knowledge and these simple tools, I believe you'd find the contradictions sorting themselves out. May I leave it with you?"
Ruth (Householder): "Sure, give it here. And I'll read it properly — I read everything properly."
Daniel (Publisher): (smiles) "I'm sure you will. Enjoy the rest of your market day."

Keys: Daniel carried out lmd lesson 4 point 3. Ruth's years of churchgoing could easily have tempted a publisher to lecture her — instead, Daniel complimented her genuine Bible-reading habit, admitted he does not know everything, and offered the tract as a tool for HER to use, not a correction for her to receive. He spoke with her respectfully, as with someone who knows her Bible better than he does. Because he was not condescending, she accepted the tract willingly.

items.title: Talk — Older Ones—You Are an Asset to the Congregation (th study 16)
items.answer:
INTRODUCTION: Connie is 83 years old. Looking back on a lifetime of serving Jehovah, she says: "I'm amazed at what I was once able to accomplish. Now age has slowed me down." Perhaps you know that feeling — or you love someone who does. Age slows the body, but it must never slow our appreciation of the value older ones bring to the congregation. Today let us consider three encouraging thoughts: what Jehovah expects of you, what you can still give to others, and how Jehovah values your faithful service.

WHAT JEHOVAH EXPECTS OF YOU: You do not have to do what you did at 25. Deuteronomy 6:5 tells us what Jehovah asks: "You must love Jehovah your God with all your heart and all your soul and all your strength." Notice that the verse does not say 'with all your former energy.' Jehovah measures what you give now against your circumstances now. When you were younger, you gave him your best then. Today, whatever you can still do, if it is your best now, then you are giving him your best — the same gift you always gave. So do not measure today against the past. Love him with all you have today, and you have met the standard.

YOU CAN GREATLY BENEFIT OTHERS: An older Christian can do something a young one cannot: speak from long experience. King David did exactly that: "I was once young and now I am old, But I have not seen anyone righteous abandoned, Nor his children looking for bread." (Ps 37:25) That statement carries weight precisely because David was OLD when he said it. Decades of watching Jehovah's care gave him something no young person could say with the same authority. If you have watched Jehovah bless his people through famines, persecutions, sicknesses and political upheavals — tell the younger ones! Paul showed us the value of this 'interchange of encouragement by one another's faith.' (Rom 1:12) Even a simple comment at the meeting, a phone call or a card can refresh someone whose faith is wavering. And do not underestimate simply being AT the meetings in person, to the extent your health allows. Connie says attending meetings keeps her from getting discouraged — and her presence keeps others encouraged too.

JEHOVAH VALUES YOUR FAITHFUL SERVICE: Think of Simeon, an elderly man who could do very little temple service — yet Jehovah saw him as 'righteous and devout' and gave him the privilege of holding the infant Jesus. (Luke 2:25-35) Jehovah looks past the ageing body and sees strong faith. Paul's words apply to you: "For God is not unrighteous so as to forget your work and the love you showed for his name by ministering and continuing to minister to the holy ones." (Heb 6:10) Notice — 'continuing to minister.' Jehovah does not forget the years; he is watching what you continue to do even now.

CONCLUSION: So if you are older: Jehovah does not measure you against your former self — he values your faithful service exactly as it is today. (2 Cor 8:12) And if you are young: treasure the older ones around you, listen to them, sit with them, benefit from them. They are not a burden on the congregation — they are its living memory and one of its greatest assets.

scriptures.quote: You must love Jehovah your God with all your heart and all your soul and all your strength.
I was once young and now I am old, But I have not seen anyone righteous abandoned, Nor his children looking for bread.
or, rather, that we may have an interchange of encouragement by one another's faith, both yours and mine.
For God is not unrighteous so as to forget your work and the love you showed for his name by ministering and continuing to minister to the holy ones.
For if the readiness is there first, it is especially acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what a person does not have.

items.title: Help Caregivers Not to Give Out
items.answer:
DISCUSSION — Caring for a sick, elderly or disabled loved one is a privilege, but it is also one of the most demanding assignments a Christian can carry. Below are prepared comments for each question in the part.

How can family members apply these scriptures when caring for loved ones? "By consultation, plans will succeed, And by skillful direction wage your war." (Prov 20:18) Caring for an elderly parent or a sick spouse is a 'war' against exhaustion — and it should not be fought alone or unplanned. Family members can sit down together and consult: who takes which day, who handles transport to the doctor, who covers meals, what is the weekly budget. A written plan shared by all prevents resentment later. And Philippians 2:4 says: "as you look out not only for your own interests, but also for the interests of others." When a brother or sister in the congregation is caring for a loved one, we look out for THEIR interests — not by waiting to be asked, but by stepping up with a specific offer: 'I will take your Tuesday meeting ride,' 'I am bringing dinner on Friday.'

What is involved in being a caregiver? It involves far more than physical tasks — bathing, cooking, medications, hospital visits. It involves emotional labour: watching a loved one decline, managing their moods and fears, and doing it all while carrying one's own responsibilities to family, work and worship. Many caregivers quietly sacrifice their own rest, personal study and ministry time. That is why we should honour them rather than assume all is well.

How can caregivers take care of themselves? Accept that self-care is not selfishness. Ask for help early, before exhaustion sets in — make a list of specific needs and share it with those who offer. Keep feeding yourself spiritually: even a shortened personal study or listening to publications while doing chores keeps your hope alive. Take real breaks when others can step in, and keep at least some direct share in spiritual activities so your joy is not entirely buried in your duties.

How can the congregation help caregivers? With practical, specific assistance: offer lifts to meetings and doctors, arrange meals, sit with the sick one for an hour so the caregiver can attend a meeting or rest, send encouragement, and — importantly — keep inviting the caregiver, never assuming they 'cannot come anymore.' Elders can give kind, non-judgmental shepherding visits. Small consistent help matters more than one grand gesture.

How does Jehovah help caregivers not to give out? Through the congregation — the practical help we just discussed is often the very channel of Jehovah's support, as this video illustrates. He also helps directly: prayer lifts the weight even when circumstances cannot change, and the hope of the new world keeps the daily grind in perspective. And the ministry, even in a small measure, reminds a caregiver that they are still useful to Jehovah. VIEW: 'Comfort for the Caregiver' — after viewing, sample comments can be refined around what the video shows: the emotional strain caregivers carry, and how Jehovah supports them through the practical kindness of fellow believers.

scriptures.quote: By consultation, plans will succeed, And by skillful direction wage your war.
as you look out not only for your own interests, but also for the interests of others.
