items.title: Congregation Bible Study — Walk Courageously With God, chap. 18
items.answer: Study source: the book Walk Courageously With God! (wcg), chapter 18, "Courageous and Cautious" — the account of Gideon (wcg chap. 18 pp. 86-89). The Bible account read: Judges 6:1–7:22; 8:4-23, 28. Below are prepared answers to every question in the chapter — the discussion question, Dig Deeper, Reflect on the Lessons and Meditate on the Bigger Picture.

cbs.label: For discussion
cbs.q: In what ways did Gideon show courage?
cbs.answer: Gideon showed courage in several ways. He tore down the altar of Baal even though fear of the townspeople moved him to do it at night — he acted despite fear, which is what courage really is. He summoned an army when the enemy filled the valley like locusts. He accepted Jehovah's drastic reduction of that army to 300 men and went ahead anyway. He crept alone into an enemy camp of 135,000 men at night to overhear the dream Jehovah had arranged. And he led a strange battle plan — jars, torches and horns — trusting that Jehovah would bring the victory. Notice that each act of courage was backed by caution: he asked for signs, he spied first, he obeyed instructions exactly.

scriptures.quote: Jehovah's angel appeared to him and said: “Jehovah is with you, you mighty warrior.”

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 1
cbs.q: Why might the “round loaf of barley” in the soldier's dream have been a fitting symbol of Gideon's army? ( Judg. 7:13 ; it “Barley” ¶7 )
cbs.answer: Barley was the bread of the ordinary farmer — the poor man's grain, harvested by common people. Gideon's army was exactly that: no professional soldiers, no fancy armour, just 300 farmers with jars and horns. Yet the little barley loaf flattened the great tent of Midian. So the symbol fit on both ends: the army looked as humble and unimpressive as a loaf of barley bread, and the victory came from Jehovah, not from military might. What looks small and ordinary in Jehovah's hands can crush what looks impressive — a lesson for us when the preaching work seems weak by this world's standards.

scriptures.quote: There was a round loaf of barley bread rolling into the camp of Midʹi·an. It came to a tent and struck it so hard that it collapsed. Yes, it turned the tent upside down, and the tent fell flat.”

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 2
cbs.q: Why did the sound of 300 horns confuse and frighten the Midianites? ( it “Horn” ¶3 )
cbs.answer: Rams' horns were used as signaling instruments — a blast was the recognized signal to attack. If a battle signal sounded, it meant an army was there. One horn might be an oddity, but 300 horns blasting at once from the darkness told the sleeping Midianites that a large attacking force had surrounded their camp. Then came the shattering jars, blazing torches on every side and the war cry 'The sword of Jehovah and of Gideon!' — Jehovah caused them to turn their swords on one another in the panic. The enemy's own ears and eyes were turned into Jehovah's weapons.

scriptures.quote: So the three bands blew the horns and shattered the large jars. They held the torches in their left hands and blew the horns in their right hands and they called out: “The sword of Jehovah and of Gidʹe·on!”

The 300 continued to blow the horns, and Jehovah turned the sword of each one against the other throughout the camp; and the army fled as far as Beth-shitʹtah, on to Zerʹe·rah, as far as the outskirts of Aʹbel-me·hoʹlah by Tabʹbath.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 3
cbs.q: What did Gideon and his army have to do to defeat the Midianites? ( w04 10/15 16 ¶9-10 )
cbs.answer: They had to obey Jehovah's instructions exactly — even when the instructions made no sense militarily. Marching to battle with jars in one hand, torches in the other and horns to blow, instead of swords; surrounding the camp in three bands; waiting in the dark for Gideon's signal; then holding position while Jehovah turned the enemy on itself. Then they had to pursue the fleeing enemy about 80 kilometres, exhausted, across the Jordan. The battle was won by faith expressed in complete obedience, not by skill with weapons. When Jehovah gives directions — in the ministry, in our trials — the winning combination is the same: precise obedience plus endurance.

cbs.label: Dig Deeper · 4
cbs.q: What details confirm the accuracy of this Bible account? ( w05 4/15 32 )
cbs.answer: The account is filled with verifiable, realistic details — the kind a forger would not invent. Gideon's army shrinks in precise stages: 32,000, then 10,000, then 300. The enemy is numbered at 135,000. The battle route is traced through real, named places — the Spring of Harod, the hill of Moreh, Beth-shittah, Zererah, Abel-meholah by Tabbath, Jogbehah. The soldier's dream, the timing of the night attack and even the aftermath — Israel's temptation to make Gideon king — all match the customs and geography of the time. Such grounded detail throughout strengthens our faith that these things really happened and that Jehovah really directed them.

cbs.label: Reflect · A
cbs.q: Gideon led God's people to a victory. But he remained humble and spoke peaceably to others. ( Judg. 8:1-3 ) How can family heads and elders imitate Gideon when someone is upset by something they do?
cbs.answer: When the Ephraimites bitterly accused Gideon of not calling them to the battle, he did not defend his record, list his achievements or match their sharp tone. He spoke humbly — 'What have I done compared with you?' — he credited Jehovah for what God had done through them, and 'when he spoke this way, they calmed down.' A family head or elder can do the same: listen fully before answering, acknowledge the person's viewpoint and feelings, avoid the instinct to win the argument, and give credit where the other person contributed. A soft, humble answer can defuse in minutes what a proud one would inflame for months.

scriptures.quote: But he said to them: “What have I done compared with you? Are not the gleanings of Eʹphra·im better than the grape harvest of Abi-eʹzer?
It was into your hand that God gave Midʹi·an's princes Oʹreb and Zeʹeb, and what have I done compared with you?” When he spoke this way, they calmed down.

cbs.label: Reflect · B
cbs.q: In what situations might we need to be both courageous and cautious? (Picture C)
cbs.answer: Whenever we take a stand for our faith. At school or work: courage to explain why we do not join certain activities, caution in choosing the right time, words and attitude. On the ministry: courage to speak up about our hope, caution to avoid stirring up quarrels over political or religious differences. Online: courage to defend the truth, caution about what we share and whom we engage. In association: courage to cut off bad associations, caution to handle it kindly. Even in a foreign land or under opposition: courage to keep worshipping, caution not to needlessly expose ourselves or our brothers to danger. Gideon's pattern — full trust in Jehovah, carefulness in the details — applies to all of these.

cbs.label: Reflect · C
cbs.q: How might you imitate Gideon's courage in your life?
cbs.answer: By praying for Jehovah's backing and then acting on it: identifying openly with Jehovah's people even when it costs us; giving a witness to a neighbour, workmate or relative we have been avoiding; standing firm at school or work when our beliefs are tested; accepting a privilege of service we feel too weak for; and refusing to give up in the face of overwhelming odds — illness, opposition or discouragement. Like Gideon, we can be honest about our fear, ask Jehovah to reassure us, and then move forward, because the victory depends on him, not on our numbers.

cbs.label: Meditate · A
cbs.q: What does this account teach me about Jehovah?
cbs.answer: It teaches me that Jehovah sees potential in people who doubt themselves — he called hiding Gideon 'a mighty warrior' and gave him the spirit to become exactly that. It teaches me that Jehovah patiently works with hesitant faith: he answered Gideon's repeated requests for signs without rebuking him. It teaches me that Jehovah deliberately shrinks our resources — from 32,000 to 300 — so that no one can credit anyone but him for the victory. And it teaches me that he honors humility: the man who refused a throne (Judg 8:23) died at a good old age and is named in Paul's list of the faithful.

scriptures.quote: But Gidʹe·on said to them: “I will not rule over you, nor will my son rule over you. Jehovah is the one who will rule over you.”

cbs.label: Meditate · B
cbs.q: How does the account tie in with Jehovah's purposes?
cbs.answer: Jehovah's victory through Gideon preserved his people and their worship in the land, keeping alive the line through which the promised Seed — the Messiah — would come. Gideon himself is a prophetic picture of the greater Deliverer: Jehovah's anointed King, Jesus Christ, who will lead a divinely chosen, seemingly small force of 144,000 to victory over all the nations in Har-Magedon. Just as the Midianites destroyed themselves while Gideon's men simply obeyed and watched, the nations at Armageddon will turn on one another while Christ's followers stand in their place under Jehovah's direction. The final outcome — peace restored to God's people — points to the Paradise under Kingdom rule.

cbs.label: Meditate · C
cbs.q: What would I like to ask Gideon in the resurrection?
cbs.answer: I would like to ask him: 'What went through your mind when you tore down that altar of Baal at night — were you more afraid of the townspeople or of Jehovah? And when Jehovah cut your army down from 32,000 to 300, how long did it take you to accept it?' I would also love to hear what he felt when the Ephraimites confronted him after the victory — and whether he knew at the time that his refusal of the throne would make him immortal in Scripture, named in Paul's list of the faithful. I suspect he would smile and say it was all Jehovah's doing from start to finish.

wt.article: How the Priesthood Reveals Jehovah’s Love

items.q: Why is mankind in dire need of help?
items.comment: In a word — sin. Because of inherited sin, the whole human family is alienated from God: "At that time you were without Christ, alienated from the state of Israel, strangers to the covenants of the promise; you had no hope and were without God in the world." (Eph 2:12) Sin has opened a chasm between us and our Creator, and no man can cross it by himself. Without help we could never find true meaning in life, and we would have no hope for the future. Our need is desperate.

scriptures.quote: At that time you were without Christ, alienated from the state of Israel, strangers to the covenants of the promise; you had no hope and were without God in the world.
scriptures.use: Shows the desperate condition: separated from God, without hope — the very chasm the priesthood arrangement is designed to bridge.

scriptures.quote: Indeed, you who were once alienated and enemies because your minds were on the works that were wicked,
scriptures.use: Adds that sin makes us not only alienated but actually enemies of God — help cannot come from our side of the gap.

items.insight: Sin is not a flaw we can self-repair — it is a chasm we cannot cross. Help has to come from God's side of the gap, and the whole priesthood arrangement proves that he crossed it first.
items.apply: This week, when a Bible truth exposes something in you, thank Jehovah that he already made the way back to him — instead of assuming you have to clean yourself up before you can approach him in prayer.

paraNotes.points: All humans, whether they know it or not, are in desperate need because of inherited sin — sin alienates mankind from God and creates a chasm man cannot cross by himself; without help there is no true meaning in life and no hope for the future.
paraNotes.highlight: Sin is described as a chasm — that picture drives this whole article: a gap only God can bridge.

items.q: What will we consider in this article?
items.comment: We will consider the priesthood arrangement — the remarkable arrangement Jehovah made to save us from our sinful state. First, how it proved a blessing for men and women in ancient times. Then how we can benefit from the priesthood arrangement that is in effect today and will continue to benefit in the future. And finally, how the whole arrangement reveals Jehovah's deep love for us. Keep that last point in mind all the way through.
items.insight: The article is really one long answer to a single question: what does a priesthood in heaven have to do with me? The answer: everything — it is the channel of God's love to imperfect humans.
items.apply: As you study this week, ask after each paragraph: how does this draw me closer to Jehovah? Let the article do what it sets out to do.

paraNotes.points: Jehovah made a priesthood arrangement — for ancient Israel and later for the Christian congregation — and it is still in effect today. The article considers how the arrangement blessed people in ancient times, how we benefit now and in the future, and how it reveals Jehovah's deep love for us.
paraNotes.highlight: The closing sentence is the real theme: the priesthood reveals his deep love.

items.q: According to Hebrews 5:1, in what way does the priesthood help sincere worshippers?
items.comment: Hebrews 5:1 explains that the high priest is appointed in behalf of men "over the things relating to God" — that is, the priesthood bridges the gap between God and man. Sin created the divide; the priesthood bridges it. Priests helped sincere worshippers approach God acceptably, and that is exactly what the great High Priest, Jesus, does for us today. Jehovah wanted Israel to draw closer to him, and the priesthood was his chosen means.

scriptures.quote: For every high priest taken from among men is appointed in their behalf over the things relating to God, so that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.
scriptures.use: The article's key text: the high priest is appointed FOR men, over the things relating to God — the channel through which worshippers approach God acceptably.

items.insight: Read Hebrews 5:1 carefully: the priest is appointed in OUR behalf. Approach to God was never left to our initiative — Jehovah made the appointment before we ever dared to come near.
items.apply: When you feel too unclean to pray, remember: Jehovah himself appointed the arrangement that lets you approach. Pray anyway — that is what the arrangement exists for.

paraNotes.points: Under inspiration Paul explains why Jehovah provided a priesthood for Israel: to help sincere worshippers draw closer to God and approach him acceptably — the priesthood bridges the gap that sin created.
paraNotes.highlight: Picture: a worshipper approaching God with the priest bridging the divide — the visual for the whole article.

items.q: How did the priests of Israel represent God before man?
items.comment: By serving as teachers. Malachi 2:7 says: "The lips of a priest should safeguard knowledge, and people should seek the law from his mouth, because he is the messenger of Jehovah of armies." The priests had the assignment to teach the Law to Israel, helping the people understand it and live by it. In Nehemiah's day, 13 Levites helped Ezra explain the Law — putting meaning into it so the people could apply it. In this way the Israelites could draw closer to God.

scriptures.quote: For the lips of a priest should safeguard knowledge, and people should seek the law from his mouth, because he is the messenger of Jehovah of armies.
scriptures.use: The priest teaches God's law to the people — the priest acting as God's representative before man.

scriptures.quote: And they continued reading aloud from the book, from the Law of the true God, clearly explaining it and putting meaning into it; so they helped the people to understand what was being read.
scriptures.use: The practical example from Nehemiah's day: Ezra and the Levites made the Law understandable so people could apply it and draw close to Jehovah.

items.insight: Representing God to man is a teaching work — and notice HOW: 'putting meaning into it.' God's truth is not meant to stay lofty; someone must make it usable at street level.
items.apply: Thank the teachers in your congregation this week — and imitate them: when you share in teaching (family worship, comments, ministry), put meaning into it, not just words.

paraNotes.points: Priests represented God before man by teaching the Law (Mal 2:7). Example: in Nehemiah's day 13 Levites assisted priest Ezra, clearly explaining the Law and putting meaning into it so the people could apply it and draw closer to him.
paraNotes.highlight: Nehemiah 8:8's phrase 'putting meaning into it' — teaching means more than reading aloud.

items.q: How did the priests of Israel represent man before God, and what does that teach us about Jehovah?
items.comment: By offering sacrifices in behalf of the people. Israelites were well aware of their daily errors and failings, and they knew they needed their sins wiped away — David prayed: "Wash away my transgression." (Ps 51:9) The priests and the sacrifices made forgiveness possible, and what a relief that was for repentant Israelites! Through the priesthood arrangement we see Jehovah's love, compassion and interest in the well-being of his people — and ultimately in their salvation.

scriptures.quote: Turn your face away from my sins, And wipe away all my errors.
scriptures.use: The cry of a repentant Israelite aware of daily failings — the felt need the sacrificial system was designed to answer.

items.insight: The second half of the priest's job is the opposite of the first: first he brought God's word down to man, then he carried man's need up to God. Jehovah built compassion into the arrangement itself.
items.apply: Identify one sin or weakness you have been carrying alone, and take it up the bridge — ask specifically for forgiveness this week, as David did.

paraNotes.points: Priests represented man before God by offering sacrifices in the people's behalf. Israelites knew their daily errors and knew they needed their sins wiped away (Ps 51:9); the sacrifices made forgiveness possible — a great relief for repentant Israelites. The arrangement displays Jehovah's love, compassion and interest in his people's salvation.
paraNotes.highlight: Ps 51:9 — the heartfelt need behind the sacrifices: not ritual, but real relief over real guilt.

items.q: In patriarchal times, what role did a family head have that was similar to that of a priest?
items.comment: Long before Israel existed, the family head offered sacrifices for himself and his household. Noah offered sacrifices of thanksgiving after leaving the ark. Abraham built altars to Jehovah. And Job offered burnt sacrifices in behalf of his children, showing that the arrangement existed before the Levitical priesthood. Jehovah even told the Israelites: "Let the priests [the family heads] who regularly come near to Jehovah sanctify themselves." (Ex 19:22) The role of priest was woven into family life from the very beginning.

scriptures.quote: Then Noah built an altar to Jehovah and took some of all the clean animals and of all the clean flying creatures and offered burnt offerings on the altar.
scriptures.use: First example of a family head acting as priest for his household — patriarchal sacrifice in action.

scriptures.quote: After a series of banquet days was complete, Job would send for them in order to sanctify them. Then he would get up early in the morning and offer up burnt sacrifices for each of them. For Job said: “Maybe my sons have sinned and have cursed God in their heart.” That is what Job would always do.
scriptures.use: Shows the depth of the family head's priestly care — sacrifices offered even for possible sins of the heart.

scriptures.quote: And let the priests who regularly come near to Jehovah sanctify themselves, so that Jehovah may not strike them.”
scriptures.use: The passage the paragraph cites — Jehovah's own words putting family heads and priests in the same category before the Levitical order existed.

items.insight: Priestly service began in the home — altars, not temples. Jehovah's pattern started with fathers caring spiritually for their households, which tells us where he expects the heart of worship to beat: in the family.
items.apply: Family heads: offer one prayer this week that follows Job's pattern — sanctifying your household before God, mentioning each member of your family by name before Jehovah.

paraNotes.points: In patriarchal times the family head offered sacrifices for himself and his family — Noah after the flood, Abraham at his altars, Job for his children. The Bible speaks of priests even before the Levitical priesthood; Jehovah told the Israelites: 'Let the priests [the family heads] who regularly come near to Jehovah sanctify themselves.' (Ex 19:22)
paraNotes.highlight: Job 1:5 — sacrifices offered not just for sins committed, but for possible sins of the heart. That is the heart of a family priest.

items.q: Who was Melchizedek, and how did he prefigure the Messiah?
items.comment: Melchizedek was the first person specifically called a priest in the Scriptures — and he was both a priest and a king. Jehovah later promised that the Messiah would be like him in that respect: "Jehovah has sworn an oath, and he will not change his mind: 'You are a priest forever In the manner of Mel·chizʹe·dek!'" (Ps 110:4) But there is one difference — the Messiah's rule will benefit mankind forever. So Jesus is both our King and our High Priest, just as Melchizedek was.

scriptures.quote: Jehovah has sworn an oath, and he will not change his mind: “You are a priest forever In the manner of Mel·chizʹe·dek!”
scriptures.use: Jehovah's oath that the Messiah would be a priest like Melchizedek — both king and priest.

scriptures.quote: For it is said in witness of him: “You are a priest forever in the manner of Mel·chizʹe·dek.”
scriptures.use: Paul applies the prophecy to Jesus — the eternal priest-king who benefits mankind forever.

items.insight: Melchizedek combines what no human system could: kingship and priesthood in one person. Only where the King is also your Priest can authority and mercy finally meet without conflict.
items.apply: When you pray in Jesus' name this week, remember you are speaking to a King-Priest — both the power to act on your behalf and the mercy to want to.

paraNotes.points: Melchizedek was the first person specifically called a priest in Scripture — and he was both a priest and a king. Jehovah promised that the Messiah would be both king and priest, as Melchizedek was — but the Messiah's rule will benefit mankind forever. (Ps 110:4; Heb 7:17)
paraNotes.highlight: The combination 'king AND priest' is the point — Israel's law never allowed one man to hold both offices.

items.q: How was the priesthood organized under the Mosaic Law?
items.comment: With the Mosaic Law, Jehovah organized the priesthood on a national scale. Aaron and his descendants were assigned to serve as priests, with the Levites assisting them, and they offered sacrifices for the nation and for individuals. Jehovah gave specific guidelines — the types of offerings, their purpose, and how they were to be presented. Moses anointed Aaron and his sons so they could serve: "their anointing will serve continually for them as a lasting priesthood during their generations." (Ex 40:15) All of it provided a foretaste of what was to come.

scriptures.quote: You are to anoint them just as you anointed their father, so that they will serve as priests to me, and their anointing will serve continually for them as a lasting priesthood during their generations.”
scriptures.use: The founding command for the Aaronic priesthood — an anointing that would last 'during their generations,' pointing to the reality to come.

items.insight: Every detail — who, what offering, how presented — came from Jehovah himself. Worship acceptable to God is not self-designed; he provides both the arrangement and the instructions for it.
items.apply: Resist the itch to fashion your own 'spirituality.' This week, let God's Word — not personal preference — set the standards for your worship.

paraNotes.points: Under the Mosaic Law, Aaron and his descendants were assigned as priests, assisted by the Levites, offering sacrifices for the nation and for individual Israelites, following Jehovah's specific guidelines on the types, purpose and presentation of offerings. The whole arrangement provided a foretaste of what was to come.
paraNotes.highlight: The organization of worship is Jehovah's, down to the details — a foretaste of the greater priesthood to come.

items.q: Who will serve as priests along with Jesus during the Thousand Year Reign?
items.comment: Jesus, our High Priest, now serves in Jehovah's great spiritual temple, appearing before God on our behalf — he gave up his perfect life to atone completely for man's sins. (Heb 9:24) Alongside him, 144,000 anointed ones will serve as kings and priests. (1 Pet 2:9) Once resurrected to heaven, they will work with God and Christ to bring obedient mankind to perfection and make the earth a paradise. Jehovah will use a priesthood throughout the Thousand Year Reign — until man no longer needs priestly services.

scriptures.quote: For Christ did not enter into a holy place made with hands, which is a copy of the reality, but into heaven itself, so that he now appears before God on our behalf.
scriptures.use: Jesus is serving right now as High Priest in heaven itself, appearing before God for us — not a past event but a present ministry.

scriptures.quote: But you are “a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for special possession, that you should declare abroad the excellencies” of the One who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light.
scriptures.use: The 144,000 are the 'royal priesthood' who will serve alongside Jesus as kings and priests in the Thousand Year Reign.

items.insight: The priesthood is not an ancient relic — it is active right now in heaven. And notice where it is heading: not endless ritual, but a definite end, when mankind is perfect and no longer needs an intercessor.
items.apply: Hear a talk or read about the heavenly hope this week and thank God that priestly help is flowing right now — then pray for the earthly subjects who will be lifted to perfection.

paraNotes.points: At his baptism Jesus became the High Priest serving in Jehovah's great spiritual temple; his sacrifice was far superior to the animal sacrifices of Israel. He continues to serve, appearing before God on our behalf (Heb 9:24). Under God's Kingdom arrangement, 144,000 anointed ones will serve alongside him as kings and priests (1 Pet 1:3, 4; 2:9).
paraNotes.highlight: Jesus' priesthood is PRESENT-TENSE — 'he now appears before God on our behalf.' He is serving for you this very day.

paraNotes.points: Jehovah has arranged for man to benefit from priestly services throughout much of history; the sacrifices reminded faithful Israelites of their need for a ransom. The priesthood will continue throughout the Thousand Year Reign until man is brought to perfection and no longer needs priestly services.
paraNotes.highlight: The arrangement has an END GOAL — perfection. Priesthood is medicine, not a permanent condition.

items.q: How does the priesthood reflect Jehovah's desire to have a close relationship with mankind?
items.comment: The priesthood shows that Jehovah is determined to close the gap that sin opened — forever. He wants us to approach him, gain his favor, enjoy a warm personal relationship with him, and be saved. (2 Cor 5:18) And here is the tender part: Jehovah realizes our sinful state is something we inherited through no fault of our own. He mercifully reaches out to each one, helping us gain an approved standing before him. Does that not move you to love him even more?

scriptures.quote: But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of the reconciliation,
scriptures.use: Reconciliation runs from God's side — he took the initiative through Christ, which is exactly what the priesthood arrangement displays.

items.insight: Jehovah treats inherited sin the way a father treats a child's inborn weakness — not as treachery but as something to be helped past. Mercy is built into his reading of our condition.
items.apply: Replace one self-condemning thought this week with the fact of verse 18: God reconciled us to himself. He did the moving; receive it rather than earn it.

paraNotes.points: The priesthood reflects Jehovah's desire for a close, personal relationship with his servants. Though sin created a gulf, he is determined to close it forever — he wants us to approach him, gain his favor and be saved (2 Cor 5:18). He mercifully reaches out to each one, knowing our sinful state was inherited through no fault of our own.
paraNotes.highlight: The paragraph ends with a question for the audience: 'Does that not move you to love him even more?' — invite a comment on it.

items.q: Why is it encouraging that Jesus, the High Priest, pleads on our behalf?
items.comment: Because as our helper with the Father, Jesus pleads for us personally (1 John 2:1; read Heb 7:25). He considers your background, upbringing, health and emotional makeup — your fine qualities, your record of faithful service, your constant prayers for forgiveness and your sincere efforts to improve. And his pleadings are well-received, because Jehovah is compassionate and ready to forgive. (Ps 86:5) Our High Priest takes into account who you really are.

scriptures.quote: So he is able also to save completely those who are approaching God through him, because he is always alive to plead for them.
scriptures.use: Jesus pleads for those APPROACHING God — the plea is continuous and effective; salvation through him is complete.

scriptures.quote: For you, O Jehovah, are good and ready to forgive You abound in loyal love for all those who call on you.
scriptures.use: Why Jesus' pleadings succeed: Jehovah is good, ready to forgive, abounding in loyal love for those who call on him.

items.insight: 'Pleads for them' is ongoing — always alive. Your worst week does not suspend the intercession; the pleading resumes every morning exactly where you are.
items.apply: Approach God through Jesus about the specific weakness you feel least able to name — that is precisely the case your Advocate is pleading.

paraNotes.points: Jesus, as High Priest, acts as 'a helper with the Father,' pleading for us (1 John 2:1; Heb 7:25). He may consider our background, health and emotional makeup, our fine qualities and deeds, our record of faithful service, our constant prayers for forgiveness and sincere efforts to improve — and his pleadings are well-received by Jehovah, who is compassionate and ready to forgive (Ps 86:5).
paraNotes.highlight: Picture: the High Priest weighing each worshipper's circumstances before Jehovah — pleadings personalized, not formulaic.

items.q: According to Hebrews 4:16, what additional blessing does the priesthood offer, and why is that so helpful?
items.comment: Open communication with God. Because of the services of our great High Priest, we can speak to Jehovah freely in prayer: "Let us, then, approach the throne of undeserved kindness with freeness of speech, so that we may receive mercy and find undeserved kindness to help us at the right time." (Heb 4:16) Even when we are so distressed we do not know what to pray for, the spirit itself pleads for us with unuttered groanings (Rom 8:26). Jehovah listens, understands, and responds. Never hesitate to share any concern with our loving heavenly Father.

scriptures.quote: Let us, then, approach the throne of undeserved kindness with freeness of speech, so that we may receive mercy and find undeserved kindness to help us at the right time.
scriptures.use: The priesthood assures open access: freeness of speech before the throne of undeserved kindness.

scriptures.quote: In like manner, the spirit also joins in with help for our weakness; for the problem is that we do not know what we should pray for as we need to, but the spirit itself pleads for us with unuttered groanings.
scriptures.use: When distress leaves us wordless in prayer, we are not left without an interpreter — help joins in at the point of our weakness.

items.insight: The blessing is not just that prayer is possible but that it is safe — freeness of speech means you can bring the unedited version of your heart to the throne.
items.apply: This week, pray one prayer with no polished phrases — tell Jehovah exactly where the hurt is. That is what 'freeness of speech' is for.

paraNotes.points: The priesthood assures us that Jehovah wants open communication with us: because of the services of the great High Priest, Jesus, we can speak to Jehovah freely in prayer — 'approach the throne of undeserved kindness with freeness of speech' (Heb 4:16). Even when distress leaves us not knowing what to pray for, the spirit pleads for us; Jehovah listens, understands and responds (Rom 8:26).
paraNotes.highlight: Rom 8:26 — help for the moment when pain outruns vocabulary.

items.q: How does the sacrifice of Jesus reflect Jehovah's interest in our eternal salvation?
items.comment: The priesthood shows that Jehovah wants us to have life: "I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that someone wicked changes his way and keeps living." (Ezek 33:11) The animal sacrifices could not completely atone for sins — the Law made nothing perfect. But they pointed to the perfect sacrifice of Christ Jesus, which makes true forgiveness possible and opens the way to everlasting life. As John writes: "he loved us and sent his Son as a propitiatory sacrifice for our sins." (1 John 4:10) Jehovah took the initiative for our salvation.

scriptures.quote: Tell them, ‘“As surely as I am alive,” declares the Sovereign Lord Jehovah, “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that someone wicked changes his way and keeps living. Turn back, turn back from your bad ways, for why should you die, O house of Israel?”’
scriptures.use: Jehovah's stated preference: life for repentant sinners — the motive behind the whole arrangement that leads to everlasting life.

scriptures.quote: The love is in this respect, not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as a propitiatory sacrifice for our sins.
scriptures.use: Love measured by who moved first: Jehovah sent his Son — salvation is his initiative, not our achievement.

items.insight: Ezekiel 33:11 reveals the heart behind the theology: Jehovah is not reluctantly forgiving — he prefers your survival to your punishment.
items.apply: If you have been postponing repentance because you fear how God will react, act on Ezekiel 33:11 this week — he is waiting for the turn, not the tribunal.

paraNotes.points: The priesthood shows that Jehovah wants us to have life (Ezek 33:11). The animal sacrifices of old did not completely atone for sins (Heb 7:19), but they pointed to the perfect sacrifice of Christ Jesus, which makes true forgiveness possible and opens the way for obedient humans to have everlasting life. Jehovah took the initiative to arrange for our salvation (1 John 4:10).
paraNotes.highlight: Note the contrast: repeated animal sacrifices that pointed forward vs. the one perfect sacrifice.

items.q: How is Jehovah's love seen in his choice of individuals who will serve as priests in the Kingdom?
items.comment: In the standard he set: like their Master, the anointed must prove faithful even to death (Phil 2:8; Rev 2:10). Their loyalty must be proved beyond all doubt before they receive such a sacred assignment. That means we can trust them to apply the benefits of the ransom sacrifice lovingly, helping us overcome sin and grow to perfection — a work that continues until Jehovah's purpose for the earth and the healing of mankind is accomplished (Rev 22:1, 2).

scriptures.quote: Do not be afraid of the things you are about to suffer. Look! The Devil will keep on throwing some of you into prison so that you may be fully put to the test, and you will have tribulation for ten days. Prove yourself faithful even to death, and I will give you the crown of life.
scriptures.use: The standard for the Kingdom priesthood: loyalty proved beyond all doubt — faithfulness even to death, tested under pressure.

scriptures.quote: And he showed me a river of water of life, clear as crystal, flowing out from the throne of God and of the Lamb
scriptures.use: The result of their completed work: the river of water of life flowing from God's throne — mankind healed.

scriptures.quote: down the middle of its main street. On both sides of the river were trees of life producing 12 crops of fruit, yielding their fruit each month. And the leaves of the trees were for the healing of the nations.
scriptures.use: The priesthood's endpoint: leaves for the healing of the nations — perfection reached, the work finished.

items.insight: A priesthood vetted by death can be trusted with your eternal future. Jehovah's love is seen not only in providing helpers but in making sure they are the kind who will never abuse the trust.
items.apply: Whatever trial tests your loyalty this week, view passing it as evidence of love, not just duty — the same proof that qualified the priests of the future.

paraNotes.points: Jehovah's love is seen in his choice of individuals who will serve as priests: like their Master, the anointed must prove faithful even to death (Phil 2:8; Rev 2:10). Their loyalty must be proved beyond all doubt, so we can trust that they will lovingly apply the benefits of the ransom sacrifice, helping us overcome sin and grow to perfection — a work continuing until Jehovah's purpose for the earth's healing is accomplished (Rev 22:1, 2).
paraNotes.highlight: The vetting standard IS the guarantee: those proved to death can be trusted with our perfection.

items.q: How does Hebrews 4:15 indicate that Jesus is uniquely qualified to serve as High Priest for us?
items.comment: Because he lived our life. "For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who has been tested in all respects as we have, but without sin." (Heb 4:15) Tired? Jesus sat exhausted by a well. Hungry and thirsty? He felt both. Opposed and ridiculed for his faith? He endured it. He even lost loved ones — his friend Lazarus and apparently his stepfather Joseph. Our High Priest cares for us with understanding and empathy that come from real experience.

scriptures.quote: For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who has been tested in all respects as we have, but without sin.
scriptures.use: The article's key verse: a High Priest tested in ALL respects as we are — sympathy built on experience, not theory.

scriptures.quote: In fact, Jacob’s well was there. Now Jesus, tired out as he was from the journey, was sitting at the well. It was about the sixth hour.
scriptures.use: Concrete proof of the sympathy: even Jesus got tired — our physical exhaustion is something he knows from the inside.

items.insight: 'Tested in all respects' makes Jesus' sympathy experiential — he is not merely informed about human suffering; he has the scars of it.
items.apply: Bring the struggle you feel most embarrassed about to Jesus in prayer this week — tiredness, hunger for relief, grief — the one thing he cannot be out of touch with.

paraNotes.points: Christ, our High Priest, is sympathetic to our challenges and experiences because he himself lived as a human on earth (Heb 4:15). Do you feel tired at times? Jesus did (John 4:6). Hunger and thirst, opposition and ridicule, loss of loved ones — he knew all of it. Our High Priest cares for us with understanding and empathy that come from experience.
paraNotes.highlight: A string of 'Have you...? Jesus did too.' — good springboard for comments: match his experiences to ours.

items.q: Why can we be sure that the anointed will have fellow feeling and insight as they help mankind?
items.comment: Because they were once exactly what we are — imperfect and sinful men and women. They know what it feels like to make mistakes and struggle with guilt, what health problems are like, both physical and emotional. And they come from a variety of backgrounds, races, cultures, time periods and personal circumstances. Whatever your life experience has been, someone from among the 144,000 can relate. They will shepherd mankind with the empathy of people who lived the struggle.
items.insight: Empathy in the new world will not be theoretical: the priests of that future were patients of the same disease first. No future worshipper will need to explain what sin feels like.
items.apply: Take comfort in your own imperfect past this week: the very experiences you regret are becoming the credentials of those who will help you — and the seed of your own compassion now.

paraNotes.points: The 144,000 will have fellow feeling and insight as they help Jesus lift mankind to perfection: they were once imperfect and sinful as men or women on earth. They know what it feels like to make mistakes, struggle with guilt and suffer physical and emotional health problems — and they come from a variety of backgrounds, races, cultures, time periods and circumstances. Whatever your life experience has been, someone among the 144,000 can relate.
paraNotes.highlight: No scripture cited in this paragraph — it stands on the logic of shared experience.

items.q: What does the priesthood teach us about Jehovah's personality, and how does that make you feel about him?
items.comment: It teaches that love, mercy, compassion and fellow feeling are real aspects of Jehovah's personality. And consider the contrast the paragraph draws: Satan is our constant accuser; Jehovah is not (Rev 12:10). All through this study we have seen how Jehovah has done much to draw us to him and to pave the way for us to feel assured of his approval and friendship. Does that not draw you closer to him? Does it not make it easier to accept his love and forgiveness?

scriptures.quote: I heard a loud voice in heaven say: “Now have come to pass the salvation and the power and the Kingdom of our God and the authority of his Christ, because the accuser of our brothers has been hurled down, who accuses them day and night before our God!
scriptures.use: The contrast: 'the accuser of our brothers' accuses day and night — Jehovah, by contrast, builds the arrangement that defends and forgives us.

items.insight: Two voices compete for the microphone over your conscience: the accuser who rehearses your failures day and night, and the Provider who built a bridge past them. The priesthood identifies which one is lying.
items.apply: When the replay of past sins starts up this week, name it for what it is — accusation, not conviction — and answer it with Hebrews 4:16.

paraNotes.points: All that we have learned about the priesthood teaches that love, mercy, compassion and fellow feeling are aspects of Jehovah's personality. Satan is our constant accuser; Jehovah is not (Rev 12:10). Jehovah has done much to draw us to him and to pave the way for us to feel assured of his approval and friendship.
paraNotes.highlight: Ends with two audience questions — 'Does that not draw you closer?' / 'easier to accept his love and forgiveness?' — invite comments on both.

items.q: How does the priesthood assure us that Jehovah understands the struggle we face?
items.comment: Because he knows what we are made of: "For he well knows how we are formed, Remembering that we are dust." (Ps 103:14) Even when we feel unworthy because of our sins, Jehovah understands our struggle. He looks past our sins to the good in us and our potential for improvement. And when sins and mistakes are all we can see, we need to remember: "God is greater than our hearts and knows all things." (1 John 3:20) His verdict on us is more accurate than our own.

scriptures.quote: For he well knows how we are formed, Remembering that we are dust.
scriptures.use: Jehovah's diagnosis of our material: dust — his expectations are calibrated to what we actually are.

scriptures.quote: regarding whatever our hearts may condemn us in, because God is greater than our hearts and knows all things.
scriptures.use: When our own heart condemns us, God knows more about us than our heart does — including the good we cannot see.

items.insight: When your heart condemns you, it is overreaching — it is not the judge. God is greater than your heart; his full-file knowledge includes the good you cannot see.
items.apply: Write down three things Jehovah sees in you that your discouragement hides, and thank him for them in prayer this week.

paraNotes.points: Our study of the priesthood assures us that even when we feel unworthy because of our sins, we can trust that Jehovah understands our struggle — he knows that we are made of dust (Ps 103:14). He continues to see past our sins, focusing on the good in us and our potential for improvement; 'God is greater than our hearts and knows all things' (1 John 3:20).
paraNotes.highlight: 1 John 3:20 — the verse for the week when self-condemnation hits: God's file is more complete than our conscience.

items.q: Why are you thankful for the priesthood, and what are you determined to do?
items.comment: Because the gap between Jehovah and his imperfect but faithful worshippers has been closed. It is his heartfelt desire that we worship him acceptably, and thanks to the priesthood we can. So we do as Hebrews 4:16 encourages: "Let us, then, approach the throne of undeserved kindness with freeness of speech, so that we may receive mercy and find undeserved kindness to help us at the right time." Let us keep approaching that throne — with freeness of speech — all week long.

scriptures.quote: Let us, then, approach the throne of undeserved kindness with freeness of speech, so that we may receive mercy and find undeserved kindness to help us at the right time.
scriptures.use: The article's closing invitation: keep approaching the throne — mercy and help at the right time are waiting there.

items.insight: The article ends where worship begins: at the throne. Everything the priesthood achieved collapses into one habit — approaching with freeness of speech.
items.apply: Turn this study into a habit before it fades: choose a fixed daily time this week to approach the throne in prayer, and protect that appointment.

paraNotes.points: Jehovah has provided the priesthood so that we can worship him acceptably — it is his heartfelt desire that we do so. Thanks to this gift, the gap between Jehovah and his imperfect but faithful worshippers has been closed. We may thus approach the throne of undeserved kindness with freeness of speech, to receive mercy and find undeserved kindness to help at the right time (Heb 4:16).
paraNotes.highlight: The whole study lands on the model-prayer privilege: the bridge is built; walking onto it is our move.

recap.q: In what way does the priesthood help man to worship God acceptably?
recap.comment: The high priest is appointed in behalf of men over the things relating to God. (Heb 5:1) Sin created a divide between God and man, and the priesthood bridges it: priests taught the people God's Law, and they offered sacrifices so sins could be wiped away. Today our great High Priest, Jesus, and the anointed ones with him make our approach to Jehovah acceptable and apply the benefits of his ransom sacrifice.

recap.q: How has Jehovah used the priesthood throughout the centuries?
recap.comment: In patriarchal times family heads like Noah, Abraham and Job offered sacrifices for their households. Melchizedek, both priest and king, prefigured the Messiah. Under the Mosaic Law, Aaron and his sons served as priests with the Levites' assistance, and those sacrifices foreshadowed the ransom. Since his baptism, Jesus has served as High Priest, and during the Thousand Year Reign the 144,000 will serve with him as kings and priests until mankind is brought to perfection.

recap.q: How does the provision of the priesthood draw you closer to Jehovah?
recap.comment: It assures us that Jehovah wants us near him: we can approach the throne of undeserved kindness with freeness of speech (Heb 4:16). Jesus, who was tested in all respects as we are, pleads for us, and Jehovah — who knows we are dust — sees past our sins to the good in us. Knowing that the way back to God has already been built moves us to draw close in prayer, accept his forgiveness, and love him in return.

daily.scripture: No one has love greater than this, that someone should surrender his life in behalf of his friends.​
daily.comment: The more we engage in Jehovah’s service, the more we will experience his support and, as a result, our confidence in him will grow stronger. ( 1 Cor. 3:9 ) Remember, though, Jehovah does not look at how much you give in comparison with what others give; he sees what is in your heart. He is pleased when he observes your heartfelt gratitude for his precious gift, the ransom. ( 1 Sam. 16:7; Mark 12:41-44 ) It is only because of the ransom that we have forgiveness of our sins, a friendship with Jehovah, and the prospect of everlasting life. May we always show our gratitude for Jehovah’s love, which moved him to make these blessings available to us. ( 1 John 4:19 ) May we also demonstrate our appreciation for Jesus, who loved us so much that he gave his human life in our behalf! w25.01 31 ¶16-18 November 23-29

daily.scripture: I was troubled all day long.​
daily.comment: Consider how the writer of Psalm 73 felt. He saw others enjoying what looked like a healthy, prosperous, and stress-free life. ( Ps. 73:3-5, 12 ) As he observed them and their apparent success, he felt that his efforts to serve Jehovah were pointless. He was “troubled all day long” by this discouraging thought. ( Ps. 73:13, 14 ) How did he deal with his troubled feelings? The psalmist went to the peaceful setting of Jehovah’s sanctuary. ( Ps. 73:16-18 ) There, he was able to think clearly. He discerned that even though the life of some might seem easy, their long-term future was precarious. With this insight, he found peace of mind, knowing that pursuing spiritual things was the very best decision. As a result, he renewed his determination to continue serving Jehovah.​— Ps. 73:23-28 . w24.10 27 ¶11-12 November 23-29

daily.scripture: May people know that you, whose name is Jehovah, you alone are the Most High over all the earth.​
daily.comment: Jehovah has called us to be his “witnesses.” ( Isa. 43:10-12 ) Some years ago, a letter from the Governing Body stated: “The greatest honor that any of us could enjoy is that of being called one of Jehovah’s Witnesses.” Why is that so? Consider an illustration. If you needed someone to be a character witness for you in a court case, you would choose someone you know and trust, someone whose reputation would make his testimony trustworthy. By choosing us to be his Witnesses, Jehovah shows that he knows us well and that he trusts us to testify that he is the only true God. We feel so honored to be his Witnesses that we seize every opportunity to make his name known and to combat the many lies that have been told about him. By doing so, we live up to the name that we are so proud to bear, Jehovah’s Witnesses!​— Rom. 10:13-15 . w24.05 18 ¶13 November 23-29

daily.scripture: He cured all who were suffering.​
daily.comment: Serving others brought Jesus great joy. On one occasion when Jesus ministered to a crowd, he did more than teach them. He also cared for their physical needs. He miraculously provided food and then had his disciples distribute it. ( Mark 6:41 ) By doing so, he taught his disciples how to serve others. He also showed them that practical services are important. Imagine the joy the apostles had in sharing with Jesus in this miraculous distribution of food until “all ate and were satisfied”! ( Mark 6:42 ) Of course, this was not the only time that Jesus put the welfare of others ahead of his own. He used his entire earthly life to serve people. ( Matt. 4:23 ) Jesus found joy and satisfaction in teaching others and in humbly caring for their needs. w24.11 16 ¶10-11 November 23-29

daily.scripture: In the last days critical times hard to deal with will be here.​
daily.comment: As conditions in “the last days” get worse, we will no doubt have more opportunities to render aid to one another. We can also provide an emotional and spiritual haven for our brothers. One way we can do that is by making them feel welcome at the Kingdom Hall. So when our brothers and sisters attend meetings, we want to do all we can to make them feel loved, refreshed, and secure. Elders can become a refuge to those in the congregation who endure literal or figurative storms. During disasters and medical emergencies, elders take the initiative to arrange practical assistance. They also offer spiritual help. Brothers and sisters will be inclined to approach an elder if he is known to be gentle, empathetic, and willing to listen. Such qualities help others feel cared for; thus, it is easier for them to apply any Bible-based guidance an elder may provide.​— 1 Thess. 2:7, 8, 11 . w24.06 29 ¶12-13 November 23-29

daily.scripture: He did not even spare his own Son.​
daily.comment: Let us not think that because God is almighty, he does not have feelings! We are made in his image, created with the ability to feel, so it stands to reason that Jehovah has feelings. The Bible describes him as feeling “hurt” and “grieved.” ( Ps. 78:40, 41 ) Jehovah must have felt grieved as he observed his Son being cruelly tortured to death by ungodly men! The ransom teaches us that no one loves us as much as Jehovah does​—not even our dearest relative or best friend. ( Rom. 8:32, 38, 39 ) No doubt Jehovah loves us more than we love ourselves. Do you want to live forever? Not as much as Jehovah wants you to. Do you want to have your sins forgiven? Not as much as Jehovah wants to forgive them. All he asks is that we accept his gracious gift by exercising faith and being obedient. The ransom is truly a profound expression of God’s love.​— Eccl. 3:11 . w25.01 22-23 ¶8-9 November 23-29

daily.scripture: Keep on making sure of what is acceptable to the Lord.​
daily.comment: We all make some decisions based on what we perceive with our physical senses. But our physical senses can sometimes deceive us. Even when they do not, if we walk only by sight, we may end up ignoring God’s will or counsel. ( Eccl. 11:9; Matt. 24:37-39 ) When we walk by faith, however, we will more likely make decisions that are “acceptable to the Lord.” Following God’s advice will give us inner peace and make us truly happy. ( Ps. 16:8, 9; Isa. 48:17, 18 ) And if we continue walking by faith, we will have an everlasting future. ( 2 Cor. 4:18 ) How can we tell if we are walking by faith or by sight? Basically, it comes down to this: What factors guide our decisions? Are we guided only by the things we can see? Or are we guided by our trust in and advice from Jehovah? w25.03 20-21 ¶3-4 November 23-29
